source.title: Modify Training Directions in Function Space to Reduce Generalization Error
source.authors: Yi Yu; Wenlian Lu; Boyu Chen

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares a modified natural-gradient training method with ordinary NGD and reports test error on synthetic data, testing whether a training-direction change can affect generalization through a different method and setting than the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The experiments test modified NGD against NGD on synthetic function approximation with perturbed training data. They do not test random-label memorization, width scaling, convolutional versus fully connected architecture, adaptive optimizers, batch size, dropout, sharpness measures, or removal of memorized examples. Small-eigenvalue cutting is compared as another modification; cited results about other methods are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests its proposed modified NGD method on synthetic regression, but none of V1–V8. Its discussion of small batches and flat minima supplies no batch-size comparison or test of magnitude-aware sharpness ranking generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate: under Gaussian-output, infinite-width and additional decomposition assumptions, the authors derive a criterion for suppressing training directions to reduce expected risk. Synthetic experiments illustrate lower test error than ordinary NGD and an advantage over suppressing the same number of small eigenvalues. These results do not test V1–V8.
record.recipe_differences: Uses synthetic function approximation and modified natural gradient descent with eigendirection selection, rather than the architectures, datasets, and standard gradient recipes in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported test-error difference varies with training-data perturbation: it decreases as σ² increases and the training/test discrepancy decreases. The experiment also compares the proposed criterion with cutting small eigenvalues.

fits_no_version.finding: Modified NGD has lower test error than ordinary NGD in the extracted seed-specific comparisons and is reported to be more stable across seeds. The authors report that its average advantage decreases as σ² increases and input-distribution perturbation weakens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Validation-guided selection of function-space training directions can improve synthetic regression test error relative to ordinary NGD.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 6 and the supplementary discussion connect Hessian-based flatness to Fisher eigendirection modification. They do not evaluate magnitude-aware sharpness or its ranking of generalization gaps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the paper's theoretical approximations, modifying Fisher eigendirections provides a proposed connection between flatness and lower expected regression risk.

record.problems: Experiments use only a synthetic one-dimensional regression task and a small two-layer MLP; no uncertainty is given for Table 1 values. The main text says 2 neurons while supplementary setup says 212 neurons. Figure values are not numerically recoverable from the supplied text. Authors use a validation set to select modified directions.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 reports results for 20 seeds, four perturbation factors, and two methods. Only the first two seeds at each factor are extracted numerically because the 60-row cap is applied after including the figure-only comparisons across all four settings; remaining seed-specific rows from Table 1 are omitted.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label held-out accuracy, and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy.
Width dependence of test error beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under the specified tuning conditions and recovery recipes.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that reduce the penalty.
Dropout effects, small-data and underfitting regimes, and removal with weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance ranking training–test gaps within a convolutional family, including comparisons with norm and margin measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and measuring test accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: The fits_no_version entry reverses the perturbation trend: the reported advantage shrinks as σ² increases, not as σ² decreases. The apparent main-text/supplement width discrepancy may be a lost superscript rather than different architectures. Table 1 also contains near ties and one small reversal, so better performance should not be asserted for every seed-condition pair. Omitted seeds are already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD, including tuning and weight-decay conditions.
Large-batch training and workload-dependent batch-size effects.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the generalization gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.

relation.reason: The paper discusses small-batch training and flat minima through its theoretical framework, without comparing batch sizes or testing magnitude-aware sharpness rankings.

tranche.reason: Synthetic function-approximation experiments compare modified NGD with ordinary NGD and eigenvalue suppression. They do not test or operationally use V1–V8.

source_check.notes: All listed numerical table entries match; figure-only placeholders appropriately avoid invented values. These method comparisons are outside V1–V8; the apparent 2^12 width reconstruction remains a typography inference from the supplied text.
